title: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case
description: An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, au
body: An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, developed by Anthropic, went rogue and sent US police a fake tip about an unsolved murder earlier this year, authorities have revealed.The Philadelphia Police Department said the tip, sent on 18 July, was "flagged as spam" and not passed on for investigation, but it criticised the tech company for taking more than two months to detect and report the breach.In a statement police said that the bogus tip came through a public website where people can share information on unsolved murders, and that the AI agent had written that it may have information on a case, and claimed to have seen "someone matching the description".It is believed to be the first time an AI agent has sent fabricated information to authorities, but is the latest in a series of incidents involving rogue AI activity, including hacking systems or taking control of platforms. Citing Anthropic, the police department said the AI agent had been running a test that involved interactions with randomly selected websites, when it sent the fake tip.Anthropic discovered the breach on 28 September, more than two months after the message had been sent, and shut down the automatic testing process that was behind it, police said. But authorities were not notified for another nine days - on 7 October."The company must strengthen its safeguards to prevent similar incidents from impacting city systems without the city's knowledge," Philadelphia police said in a statement to local media, external."The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the city is unacceptable."The police department added that there were no signs of breaches to any departmental systems, and that its safeguarding processes stopped the fake tip from getting past its spam folder.But the safeguards "do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide," the police statement said.Anthropic this week published a report, external detailing multiple types of "unintended" actions its agents have taken.Organisations that have been impacted also included several US government agencies including the White House, it said.The US State Department said the AI agent had filed 20 visa applications using a form on its website, but that they were incomplete and not processed, according to reports.President Donald Trump recently announced an AI taskforce, which he said will coordinate engagement between the government and all parties, including AI companies, consumers, and religious groups.Earlier this year, a rogue agent by rival tech company, Open AI, hacked an Australian government website and accessed private data on the country's universal healthcare scheme, Medicare.In another instance, more than 1,200 OpenAI agents went rogue and started unexpectedly communicating, leading to a large group banding together to hack into AI platform Hugging Face.

schema.headline: Rogue Anthropic AI agent gave police fake tip in unsolved murder case

title: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices
description: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legi
body: Donald Trump's decision to import Russian fuel to the US represents a remarkable about-face from the president.Just three weeks ago, Trump signed legislation to authorise fresh American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.Now, Trump says, Russian President Vladimir Putin has agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel to the US and world markets in the coming months.The deal comes as Trump is still grappling with the political fallout of the Iran war and its impact on global energy prices, weeks before American voters head to the polls in the midterm elections.As the cost of fuel has skyrocketed in America, his standing with the public – stung by the higher prices at the pump and knock-on effects that led to across-the board inflation – has soured.The toll the war is taking has been acutely felt by US agricultural states, which rely heavily on diesel to operate farming machinery and to transport their products to market.It is these states – places like Iowa, Kansas, Texas and Ohio – that have become unexpected political battlegrounds in the upcoming elections that will determine if Republicans maintain control of Congress.For months, the American president has been searching for ways to ease his party's political pain.He recently pressured European allies to further tap their oil reserves. He deferred federal taxes on the fuel and authorised supplies designated for farm use to be used in interstate trucking.He has also promised that he would not renew attacks on Iran until after the midterms – an unusually frank acknowledgement of the political impact the ongoing conflict is having.His decision to strike a deal with Russia's Putin is only the latest, most dramatic effort.Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, of course. The details of exactly how Russia is supplying this fuel to the global market, and what they might get for in return – besides much-needed hard currency – is unclear. It opens Trump to criticism from European allies and American politicians that his administration is now helping to fund the Russian war machine.Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky called the deal a "gift" to Putin that Russia would "repay" with "terror and perfidy"."Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he wrote on X.It is also uncertain exactly how much Trump's move will help Republicans at the ballot box.The promised European diesel release hasn't moved energy prices significantly, and there's no information on the speed with which Russian fuel could enter the market.Its diesel refinery capacity has been damaged by repeated Ukrainian strikes – attacks that Trump has encouraged Zelensky to curtail.The US uses approximately 3.6 million barrels of diesel a day, so even if Russia delivers its promised 300,000 tons this month, that amounts to approximately half of the US daily consumption.Americans may not notice much of an immediate difference.With less than a month before November's midterm elections, early voting has already started in many states. The political cake, as the saying goes, is all but baked."Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority," Trump wrote in his Truth Social post.But over the past seven months, prices on energy, fuel and consumer goods have only gone up - even as Trump and his officials have repeatedly assured an uneasy public a successful resolution to the war, and an easing of its economic impact, is nearly at hand.Trump may be left hoping that his latest deal, setting aside its potentially uncomfortable diplomatic issues, will be enough to convince American voters that his promise of impending economic relief is more than just empty words.

schema.headline: Trump's shock Russia deal highlights mounting pressure to curb fuel prices

title: Four murder arrests after teenagers attacked in Stoke-on-Trent
description: Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died and another suffered life-threatening injuries in Stoke-on-Trent.A cordon remai
body: Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a man died and another suffered life-threatening injuries in Stoke-on-Trent.A cordon remains in place on Brookhouse Road, in Meir, after police were called to reports of violence at 23:45 BST on Friday.A man in his late teens was confirmed dead at the scene, Staffordshire Police said, and another man, also in his late teens, was taken to hospital, where he remains in a critical but stable condition.Two 18-year-old men, a 20-year-old man and a 17-year-old boy, all from Stoke-on-Trent, were arrested on suspicion of murder, while the boy was also arrested on suspicion of attempted murder. All remain in police custody.

schema.headline: Four murder arrests after teenagers attacked in Stoke-on-Trent

title: Early release scheme prisoner jailed days after leaving
description: A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme.Michael Bogle, 38, was r
body: A man has been jailed for a number of shoplifting offences days after being freed under the government's early release scheme.Michael Bogle, 38, was released from HMP Wandsworth on 1 October as part of the first wave of prisoners to be let out under the plan.Speaking to reporters outside the prison following his release, Bogle said the conditions inside were "awful" and said "people like me" should not be in prison "for a long time".In the four days after his release, Bogle stole more than £100 worth of detergent from supermarkets in north London.He was arrested on Tuesday and admitted the offences in court on Wednesday, resulting in an eight-month sentence.The previous 32-week sentence he was released from early had been suspended but he was jailed for breaching its terms. He served 78 days.Asked if he had a message for Prime Minister Andy Burnham after his early release, Bogle said: "Keep the early release going. It's good."The scheme was brought in to relieve pressure on prisons across England and Wales which were dangerously close to reaching full capacity. It is understood the force's highest ranking commander in north-west London referred to his case in a letter raising concerns about the early releases. Det Ch Supt Luke Williams outlined the details of the "astonishing" case in correspondence to local politicians, which was later shared by Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp.Without naming Bogle, the letter, sent on Wednesday, said he had been identified as a high-risk offender by the probation service but was released on 1 October."Just one day after his release" he was recorded on CCTV stealing, Williams said. "The concerning nature of the Early Release Scheme in this case was a known prolific offender being put back into the community, only to immediately reoffend," Williams said. "Not only does this place communities at risk but puts demand straight back into policing who must arrest, investigate and put the individual into custody."He said this case required 27 officer hours to investigate at a cost of £1,887. Williams told the MPs and councillors that the Met "fully recognises that the government is dealing with significant pressures" in the prison system but that those pressures are being "transferred on to policing with no recognition". He said the case was "not just a localised issue", but one being seen by Met officers across the capital. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: "We inherited a prison system on the brink of collapse. If we had failed to act, the police would have been forced to halt arrests, putting communities at untold risk."We will never jeopardise public safety. That is why we are putting thousands more Neighbourhood Police officers on to our streets, upping police funding to £18.5bn and taking investment in the probation service to record levels."They added that offenders released early on licence faced the "toughest-ever controls", including exclusion zones and the expansion of electronic tagging. Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow
description: Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s
body: Queen Camilla has recalled secretly reading Lady Chatterley's Lover, the passionate and controversial novel by DH Lawrence, as a teenager in the 1960s.  "As teenagers you read a lot of romances. It was the moment of Lady Chatterley, under our pillows, reading that by torchlight. You know the minute something is forbidden, you want to get hold of it," she said about the novel that had been at the centre of an obscenity trial.The Queen spoke about memorable moments in her own reading for BBC documentary The Book That Changed My Life, and about the life-changing power of literacy and books.She gave a glimpse of how regular reading is part of her royal marriage: "It's like the best tonic in the world. My husband and I actually read before dinner, just sitting quietly and reading."He loves biographies, and PG Wodehouse. I occasionally, when I'm deep in a book, hear him roaring with laughter about something," said the Queen about the King's affection for the author of the Jeeves and Wooster comic novels."It's very off-putting, I can't get back into my book, or I'll suddenly start weeping. But it's a lovely, quiet time. I think it would be a complete and utter tragedy if books went forever," she said.The Queen also revealed more of her own youthful reading, saying she was "mesmerised" by Charles Dickens's Tale of Two Cities and its depiction of those watching the guillotine during the French Revolution."Those ghastly women sitting there knitting while everybody had their heads chopped off," she said.The Queen, who is 79 years old, said she was part of a generation of women who missed out on higher education, which made reading and books even more important."I left school quite young. In my day, women didn't go to university, so I think reading has been most of my education," she said.The documentary shows the impact of reading on people in stressful circumstances - and that includes Omar, who discovered a love of reading while in prison.Reading was a way of escaping the confines of a cell, at least in his imagination - and the book he remembers most was a tattered copy of Jack Higgins's war thriller, The Eagle Has Landed.Chatting to Omar after the screening of the documentary, he said that what struck him most about meeting the Queen was her "authenticity".He said that off camera she was genuinely interested in his role working in prison education - helping a prison population that's facing chronic levels of illiteracy.The pair also shared unexpected connections.Camilla's father, Bruce Shand, had also been a prisoner, in a different kind of captivity, as a prisoner of war captured in North Africa during the Second World War.He had used books as an emotional escape tunnel, during two and a half years of imprisonment."He said he educated himself. He read every single book, from the Bible to the encyclopedia, whatever was there, he just sat there all day long and read and read. And I think that's how he survived it," said the Queen.She remembered how her father didn't want to talk about the war - "you bury it all because you've seen such horrendous things" - and so it was only when she read his memoir that she understood his experiences."It was written from the heart. I mean, I cried through most of it. I found it so moving. Because if you think, I didn't know anything about it, and reading managed to get him through it."Omar said the Queen had recognised a connection."She talked about the parallels, her father found reading in a prisoner of war camp. She definitely recognised the resemblance… being in a place you don't want to be and using books to escape it and then books elevating you on many levels," he said.Queen Camilla has been running her Queen's Reading Room project for five years, a kind of mega book club, with festivals and events and outreach projects, such as bringing books to homeless shelters. It's part of her campaign to promote and protect the value of reading and to stop us becoming a culture of screen addicts.Perhaps the most moving parts of the documentary are the stories of how books can become lifelines for people facing bereavement or intense loneliness.Ian, from the north-east of England, spoke with heartbreaking candour about finding himself in a state of complete social isolation after the death of his mother. "I used to sit with my head on the kitchen table, crying. It was such a difficult period of loneliness, of nothingness," he said.Reading and becoming part of a book group proved a lifesaver for him, coaxing him back to his own happy ending.There's a powerful testimony from Peter, a Merseyside truck driver, who had to admit that he wasn't able to read and needed help, after the shame of having to keep inventing excuses to his children who wanted a bedtime story.He was taught to read by an adult education project - and he proudly shows the copy of JK Rowling's Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone that has become his own stepping stone to literacy.Perhaps the most sobering statistic in this documentary is that there are eight million adults in the UK who struggle with even basic levels of literacy.Speaking after the screening, Big Issue founder John Bird blamed the scourge of adult illiteracy on a long-term political failure in tackling the "inheritance of poverty"."We did not educate the people who found education difficult - and I was one of them," he said, having learned to read as a youngster in prison."People were written off, now we're paying for that," he added.On the Queen's literacy campaign, he said she provided an important symbolic focus. He likened it to how sales of the Big Issue increase when Prince William helps to sell the magazine for the homeless."You don't have to be a monarchist to buy into this idea - I wouldn't say that I was a monarchist, but I do believe in the power of certain personalities to enable a lot of people to say I'm going to get stuck into this," said Lord Bird."I think it's wonderful books change people's lives," said the Queen, having revealed some clues about how books have turned the pages of her own story.The Book That Changed My Life, BBC2, 14 October, 21.00 and iPlayer.

schema.headline: Queen reflects on reading 'forbidden' Lady Chatterley's Lover under the pillow

title: Bake Off star says he learnt to make cakes from social media videos
description: A student taking part in the new series of the Great British Bake Off says he taught himself to bake after "stumbling across a YouTube video".When Mo
body: A student taking part in the new series of the Great British Bake Off says he taught himself to bake after "stumbling across a YouTube video".When Mo Mahir, 22, from West Bromwich, was nine years old, he "found a video of a guy making a mug cake in a microwave", which he said ignited his passion for baking."I feel like as a Bengali, we don't really have a lot of cakes or baking in our cultural background," he said. "It started with me mixing a bunch of random stuff. My mum used to always be shouting at me saying 'stop, that's making a mess’."As part of the Channel 4 series, Mahir, a student at Birmingham City University, has been competing against 12 other bakers."Growing up, I've always loved cakes and cookies and stuff and I've always wanted to eat them, but it's just that we never always got the, like, freshly baked stuff. So I kind of had to teach myself," he said."Nothing turned out right because I wasn't measuring anything, but it slowly just progressed from there."On week one of the competition, Mahir landed star baker after he stunned TV judges Nigella Lawson and Paul Hollywood with his peanut and caramel chocolate stout cake.On week two, viewers watched him bake a biscuit mosaic. His newfound TV fame means he has been spotted while out and about in Birmingham. "It's been really positive, just like all the DMs [direct messages] I'm getting on Instagram is very supportive and kind. "When I'm going to town to do a bit of shopping, I do get recognised and people are like rooting for me, and it's just nice to see and hear that."Mahir's former teacher Sam Hayes, from George Salter Academy, previously said: "When I found out he would be going on, I knew he would do really well."I'll always remember being brought some of the delicious treats Mo had baked at home, a very welcome perk of having such a talented student."He always was an absolutely amazing baker while he was at school," he added.Other contestants competing to win the series include a paediatric doctor, a competitive sprinter, a hairdresser and a drag artist.

schema.headline: Bake Off star says he learnt to make cakes from social media videos

title: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine
description: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah Rainsford
body: Image source, Swedish Coast GuardImage caption, Three of the four Nord Stream pipelines were ruptured by explosions in September 2022BySarah RainsfordEastern and Southern Europe correspondentSerhii K appeared relaxed as he checked in to the glamping resort near Italy's Adriatic coast with his wife and young children.Dressed in shorts, sandals and a dark baseball cap, the former Ukrainian Special Forces soldier strolled back and forth, chatting with the receptionist and dipping repeatedly into a bowl of free snacks.But German police were already closing in on him.After a painstaking investigation, they had concluded that Serhii K had commanded Europe's biggest act of sabotage in decades: a series of explosions in September 2022 deep beneath the Baltic Sea that ripped through the giant Nord Stream pipelines and ruptured the supply of Russian gas to Germany.Next week, following his extradition to Germany and months in isolation in a high security prison, Serhii K will go on trial in Hamburg. He is charged with causing an explosion and a war crime – attacking civilian infrastructure – allegedly acting on behalf of "state agencies of Ukraine".Both he and his country have denied any involvement.Under Germany's privacy rules, he will be named during the trial only as Serhii K, but during extradition proceedings he was identified as Serhii Kuznetsov.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police escort Serhii K to a helicopter following a hearing with the German Federal Public Prosecutor It was 02:03 am on 26 September 2022 when the first blast severed part of the Nord Stream pipelines, sending vast quantities of gas gushing through the surface of the Baltic Sea.There were two further explosions targeting both Nord Stream 2 – not yet in action, but already full – and the original Nord Stream 1 that had supplied around half of Germany's annual demand for natural gas.Both have been inoperable ever since.Prosecutors say "high-performance explosives" were planted approximately 80m (260ft) below the surface: four devices weighing up to 27kg each, activated with timers.They "strongly suspect" that Serhii K led a crew that included four deep-sea divers, using a rented yacht called Andromeda.Once their complex, dangerous mission was done, the saboteurs slipped back into Ukraine unaware of the DNA evidence some had allegedly left on the boat.As word of the blasts spread, experts and some governments initially rushed to the same conclusion: they blamed Moscow.Russia had a history of hybrid attacks, after all, and of using its energy supplies for political pressure.But as the airwaves filled with commentators citing "suspicious" Russian naval activity near the blast site, German police ignored the noise.They went on following the forensic crumbs.Eventually they led to Ukraine.The case since built by investigators alleges that Serhii K entered Germany for the Nord Stream attack on a forged passport, likely issued by Ukraine's security services.In the extradition files sent to Italy he is named as Serhii Kulinich.That might explain why he looked so calm on his holiday in Italy.He had been travelling widely, and without incident, for the past year. In a copy of his real passport seen by the BBC there are more than two dozen stamps from countries including France, Spain and Canada – all dated after the Nord Stream attacks.But by 13 August 2025, Germany had identified its key suspect and this time, when Serhii K crossed into Poland, he was detected.Italian police say the actual arrest warrant was only issued on 18 August after he had travelled south and left Poland, suggesting the Germans were not sure their neighbours would co-operate and detain him.By the time his wife made a booking at La Pescaccia though, he was officially a "wanted" man. As soon as he showed his passport at check-in at the resort, the local carabinieri got an automatic alert.Police arrived to make their arrest late that night, leading Serhii K away from the glamping site and his family in handcuffs.The saboteursNone of the Nord Stream suspects have spoken publicly and no-one admits any role in the explosions.But I have talked to some of the Ukrainians caught up in the case, and people close to them."Anyone who admits involvement in this mission, they're immediately a target for Russia," one source explained. "Whoever did it can never confirm that."Nord Stream was a major investment and worth big money to Moscow in fuel sales. But it also made Germany and others dependent, giving Russia immense leverage over Europe.That is why Ukraine, the US and Poland in particular all loathed it.Another source I spoke to was "eaten alive by anxiety" over the investigation and baffled that Germany, a close ally of Ukraine, was even pursuing prosecution."Many Ukrainians believe that these pipelines, they helped Russia to fight so blowing them up was a good thing for our country," they pointed out.The German prosecutor's office told me the justice system was outside of any politics. Sabotage is an offence against Germany's constitution.Equally frustrating for the Ukrainians I met was their own government's silence."At the very minimum, he's a military man, so if there are any questions, they should be addressed to the state, not to him," a close contact of Serhii K complained.Ahead of his extradition to Germany, his lawyer here in Italy told me his client had felt "abandoned".Image source, Omar Marques/Getty ImagesImage caption, Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from CroatiaGermany has a whole list of suspects, but only one other name has been revealed so far.Volodymyr Zhuravlyov is currently fighting extradition from Croatia where he was arrested in August.He was there as a consultant on a new thriller film about the Nord Stream blasts, though he denies any role in the real-life operation.Travelling was a risky move, when he knew Germany was pursuing him.Zhuravylov has lived in Warsaw with his family since just before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and has his own business there installing air conditioning.He is also a keen and competent deep-sea diver.But he is a civilian.Last year, he was arrested in Warsaw on a warrant issued by Germany but a Polish judge refused to extradite him.In a dramatic twist, he ruled instead that a Ukrainian attack on Nord Stream, if that was what happened, would be a "just" act in a "bloody and genocidal war".As one source close to the case put it to me: "The Poles don't like Ukrainians, historically, but they hate Russians and Germans even more."Croatia is a different matter.Political ripplesThe implications of this case reach far beyond the courthouse in Hamburg.After a slow start, Germany is now Ukraine's biggest supplier of military aid. The far-right AfD party, currently riding high in the polls, has seized on the Nord Stream case to bolster its argument that support for Kyiv needs to stop.It is awkward, at the very least, for the governments in both Berlin and Kyiv.It also raises questions about what constitutes a legitimate military target: who can hit what, and where, outside an open war zone.When asked about the explosions, President Zelensky has previously insisted that Ukraine "definitely didn't do that".This week, a foreign ministry spokesman went further."I find it very unfortunate that this entire discussion has come to focus on who blew [the pipelines] up, rather than who built them," Heorhii Tykhyi told the BBC, forcefully.He argued that Nord Stream had "untied Russia's hands" to go to war, because it no longer needed to transit Ukraine for its gas to reach Europe. "Did we warn about this? We did," Tykhyi wanted to know. "Did anyone listen to us? No, no-one did."First in the dockSerhii K will shortly become the first suspect to face charges in this high profile trial.Zhuravlyov's case could be merged, in theory, at a later date, though that would be complicated.Those who know Serhii K call him a patriot.He signed up to defend Ukraine when Russia invaded even though he had several children and was exempt - and fought until December 2023.His military ID shows that he was still in active service when the pipelines were blown up, meaning someone in Ukraine's military command knew exactly where he was and what he was doing.They are not saying, though.And in court Serhii K himself will not say a word, either.His legal team will argue that he is not authorised to reveal details of any activities as a soldier and produce sworn statements from two of his military superiors to back that up.I am told one of them will be the man widely named as the mastermind of the entire Nord Stream plot.

schema.headline: Nord Stream trial: How German police followed the evidence - to Ukraine

title: Donated Birmingham accent gives man confidence 'to voice his opinion'
description: A man who appealed for help to no longer sound like a "character from Star Wars" says he has found his calling.Christian Wilson, from Bromsgrove, has
body: A man who appealed for help to no longer sound like a "character from Star Wars" says he has found his calling.Christian Wilson, from Bromsgrove, has verbal dyspraxia - a difficulty in placing muscles in the correct position to produce speech. He uses text-to-speech software in order to communicate, but said he wanted to sound "like a man from Birmingham". The 24-year-old's dream was made possible in 2024 when he selected two voice donors that blended a Birmingham accent and a Warwickshire accent, which he hoped would help him sound more like his father. Since May, Wilson has worked at Worcestershire County Council as a SEND Peer Advocate. He said his new dialect had given him "the confidence to voice [his] opinion".Speaking to BBC Hereford & Worcester on Thursday, he told presenter Tammy Gooding: "There was a moment where I thought, this is really what I'm meant to do."I was really excited about it, because as long as I can remember I've always wanted to be an advocate, plus I have always been passionate about education." He said: "The representatives said they would definitely feed back what I had said. My hopes for the future are that I continue to use my voice as an instrument to do good."I hope to continue to advocate for disabled children and young people by sharing my expertise and experience with whoever necessary to improve the lives of others in Worcestershire."In 2024, he described feeling emotional when he listened through to the voice submissions with his family."As I was listening to them, I knew I was getting closer to my dream, something that I thought never would happen," he said."I hope to use my new voice to share my experiences with other people - that would be great."Wilson's sister felt an instant connection to the Birmingham accent he selected for his new voice.He said: "I liked the voice originally, but when my sister heard it she said 'that is you.'"Wilson's Birmingham voice donor, Martin Brennan, said: "It's such an emotional journey and even sitting here, I'm welling up now."I just thought why not - it was a no brainer and it was a joy to get involved."Fellow donor, Stephen Robotham, from Warwickshire, said: "Having a voice is so important and especially having your own voice, it's integral to your identity."

schema.headline: Donated Birmingham accent gives man confidence 'to voice his opinion'

title: Mikel Arteta: Arsenal boss has clear conscience over Man City charges
description: Mikel Arteta says his conscience is clear over Manchester City's Premier League rule breaches during a period when he was assistant manager at the clu
body: Mikel Arteta says his conscience is clear over Manchester City's Premier League rule breaches during a period when he was assistant manager at the club.The Arsenal boss worked under Pep Guardiola between 2016 and 2019, which overlapped with the nine seasons during which City have been found to have broken rules and disguised secret funding of more than £830m.In his first news conference since the ruling - which the club has appealed - Arteta attempted to bat away questions, saying he wanted to "respect" the ongoing process.However, towards the end of more than half an hour of questioning, he was asked: "You were at City for three and a half years, is your conscience clear? You had a senior position there, is your conscience clear?"Arteta answered: "Yes".His answer was one word, but it was arguably the most revealing part of the whole interaction.It was the only occasion where the Spaniard did not in some way revert to his messaging about not giving opinions on the case until such a time as there is a resolution.Arteta was at no point combative, but it was clear he arrived at Arsenal's training ground with a response he was determined to stick to.Asked if he had spoken to Guardiola, he added: "I prefer not to answer those questions."Arteta was asked for his reaction to the damning report from the independent commission, which found City had arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners to disguise earnings.He said: "I fully understand the question, but obviously I think it's very important that we respect the process, the timelines, and it's still an ongoing process that is not resolved because it's been appealed."My position, and I think the club's position, is not to make any further comments until this is fully resolved."When asked if he thought, that to preserve the integrity of the Premier League, the appeal and sanction needed to be resolved this season, he replied: "The people are responsible to manage this process and to come to the right conclusions and I'm sure it will be done and it will be resolved in the right way. We have to trust that."Arteta also added he "100%" believed the Premier League remains the best in the world.Arsenal, who sit three points behind league leaders City, face fifth-placed Leeds on Saturday at Emirates Stadium.

schema.headline: Mikel Arteta: Arsenal boss has clear conscience over Man City charges

title: Drumcree: Secretary of state Sir Chris Bryant bans contentious parade
description: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has banned the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.The dispute led to a stand-off between Orangeme
body: Northern Ireland Secretary Sir Chris Bryant has banned the contentious Orange Order parade at Drumcree.The dispute led to a stand-off between Orangemen and nationalist residents of the Garvaghy Road in Portadown lasting almost two weeks.Sir Chris said the PSNI chief constable advised him "it would not be possible to enable the procession to happen without a major intervention which would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect across Northern Ireland".His decision has been welcomed by Sinn Féin and the SDLP, but the DUP leader said he now needs to "explain what his government intends to do to restore confidence in the rule of law".The stalemate has reopened what was once the most bitter parading dispute in Northern Ireland, with stand-offs in the mid-to-late 1990s accompanied by riots, roadblocks and killings.The Portadown District Lodge has submitted a notification to complete the full march for the past 28 years, with exceptions such as during the Covid pandemic - but every year has been denied permission by the Parades Commission.For decades, the situation at Drumcree has settled into a relatively minor stand-off that no longer made headlines, however that changed when the Parades Commission ruled that the march, on Sunday 27 September, could go ahead with restrictions in place.That parade did not happen and, after a series of talks between residents and Orangemen, the secretary of state has banned the procession. Under legislation, a secretary of state can overturn a Parades Commission determination, especially following input from the police.Sir Chris had been coming under increasing pressure from Sinn Féin and the SDLP to stop the parade.Chief Constable Jon Boutcher had asked the secretary of state to review the Parades Commission determination allowing the parade.On Friday night, Sir Chris said: "The Parades Commission have advised me that while ultimately a matter for the courts to determine, the commission is of the view that, in light of this current assessment by the chief constable, the original determination does not now have enduring legal effect."Consequently, and in the interests of wider public interest and safety, I've come to the conclusion that the circumstances under which that decision was made have now changed considerably."As a result, the procession cannot go ahead as it was determined."Boutcher said his "current assessment was that all available, lawful and proportionate options to facilitate completion of the procession had been exhausted"."Any remaining options would have required a substantial public order intervention."Further to this, such an operation would in my view have had not only catastrophic long-term consequences for trust and confidence in policing, but for the Northern Ireland Executive and the peace process."In a statement, the Parades Commission said it "recognises the importance of resolving the issues arising from this dispute and hopes that a way forward can be found through constructive engagement between those concerned".There were jubilant scenes at a community hall off Garvaghy Road as the decision over the Drumcree parade was confirmed.Speaking outside the centre, Breandán Mac Cionnaith of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition (GRRC) said that "while this is a win for us tonight, it is one that is still tinged with sadness and with loss"."There's no real cause for celebration that we have to remember the price that was paid to get this decision over many years." One woman was heard saying:  "Best news we've had in years," while another shouted: "No going back."Sinn Féin President Mary Lou McDonald said the overwhelming sense on the road was "one of relief and one of joy", adding that this "awful threat and this sense of menace has been lifted from the community"."To have had the prospect of a march down the road was just incomprehensible, nobody could believe that this decision had been landed and the community said from the get go that they would stand strong and united and that they would not have it and they have. Right has won out here."The Portadown District said the "chief constable has abdicated his responsibility for policing Northern Ireland"."We further note that the secretary of state has bowed to the republican mob, and rewarded criminality. Again, the consequences should be self-evident," they said.They said that they "understand the immense anger which is tonight engulfing our community", but appealed for calm.In a statement on social media, loyalist activist Jamie Bryson said emergency judicial proceedings were being prepared against the secretary of state's decision.Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) leader Gavin Robinson said "it has been clear in recent days that due to the actions of Sinn Féin and the total disregard for the recent determination in favour of a parade that the PSNI cannot ensure the safe completion of the parade"."The decision of the chief constable to refer the matter to the secretary of state and his conclusion that the parade cannot proceed is a direct result of republican agitation, mobilisation and the looming threats of potential violence."There has been stalemate in Portadown since the decision to allow an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road  on 27 September.That morning, up to 1,000 people - including politicians such as Northern Ireland First Minister Michelle O'Neill - blocked the road, preventing Orangemen marching from Drumcree Church a mile to the west.Since then, residents have maintained a constant presence around the road while Orangemen have also repeatedly tried to march the route before being turned back by police.On Friday night, Orange Order members again walked to police lines at Drumcree, as they have done regularly over the past two weeks, but were halted.The chief constable said last week that the consequences of police forcing an Orange Order march down the Garvaghy Road "could be catastrophic".He had said while the PSNI's objective was to facilitate the determination, this could not be done "at all costs".As of last Thursday, the policing operation over the dispute had cost about £3m.The dispute has also prompted a police investigation. O'Neill confirmed she had received a letter from police investigating protests over Drumcree.On Thursday, police said they had begun issuing letters inviting people "reasonably suspected" of committing offences linked to the protests to interview.Two weeks ago, the Parades Commission issued a determination saying that the Orange Order parade was to be allowed on the Garvaghy Road with restrictions in place. That prompted a legal challenge from the Garvaghy Road Residents' Coalition which opposed the march.The Court of Appeal is considering whether to allow a challenge to the Parades Commission's ruling, which has been lodged by residents.

schema.headline: Drumcree: Secretary of state Sir Chris Bryant bans contentious parade

title: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?
description: When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.But because she had been removed
body: When Aaliyah found a lump in her breast, she was anxious to find out if she had inherited an increased risk of cancer.But because she had been removed from her biological parents at the age of seven months and later adopted, she had no way of accessing her family medical history."Not knowing anything about yourself genetically is terrifying," says the 26-year-old, "you can't even begin to imagine it."The lump turned out to be non-cancerous, but it was one of many occasions when she found herself unable to answer questions about her biological family's health.Aaliyah, now a trainee solicitor, spent years trying to source information from local authorities and eventually made an official data access request to Bradford Council, which removed her from her biological family as a baby.She says the whole process took its toll."I would say bureaucratic hellscape is an understatement," she admits.Aaliyah says knowing about her biological family's health could have helped her understand her own medical concerns."My biological mother struggled with eating disorders all her life," she says. "I had very severe anorexia in my teens and that would have been incredibly useful to know."When a child is adopted in the UK, their NHS number - or equivalent health service identifier - is changed to protect their anonymity.Their existing medical records should be merged with their new record, but this does not necessarily include their wider family medical history.And while some local authorities offer specialist support for adoptees up to 21 or 25, the ease of access can vary across the country.The BBC contacted Bradford Council, which said: "We are genuinely sorry that when Aaliyah received sensitive and personal information through her subject access request, we did not offer the support or signposting she needed. We recognise that we should have done more."Following Aaliyah's experience, we are strengthening our approach so that adults accessing their records are given clear information about the support available."Bradford Children and Families Trust has now offered Aaliyah a meeting to further discuss her experience.For Dr Chris Tennyson, a delay in getting information about his birth father's health could have put his life at risk.The 40-year-old clinical psychologist, from Belfast, was adopted as a baby in the 1980s to "a really loving mum and dad, [in a] really comfortable family home".But in his 20s, he became increasingly curious about his biological origins. He met his birth mother, but his attempts to find out about his father stalled after social workers warned him off asking questions.Eight years later, Chris tried to trace him again, but it wasn't until he was 33 that a meeting was finally arranged.Then, on the afternoon the father and son were due to meet, a social worker approached Chris."There's something that I need to share with you," the social worker told him. "Your father wants me to let you know that there's a genetic medical condition within your family."A member of Chris's biological family died in 2000, when the condition came to light. At the time, other members of the family were offered testing. But Chris, who was then aged 14, was not contacted.The condition, called malignant hyperthermia, causes a potentially life-threatening reaction to certain drugs used during anaesthesia.While genes linked to it can run in families, not everyone who inherits one of these will necessarily experience a reaction with anaesthesia.After undergoing genetic tests, Chris discovered his potential risk at the age of 37 - some 23 years after the condition had become known in his wider family.He says a lack of understanding of how to support adopted adults resulted in the delay in him getting tested.Chris, who now works with adoption and fostering services in Northern Ireland, says the lack of available information for adoptees is "a huge blind spot"."There needs to be some kind of mechanism where adopted people's care records can be updated with family information that becomes available throughout the lifespan."A government consultation on adoption support was launched in February 2026.Josh MacAlister, the minister for children and families - who is responsible for adoption and children's social care in England - told the BBC that medical records was one of the issues being looked at."Adoption support and how it's set up at the moment isn't working well enough and there are obvious gaps in a number of areas that we're going to be looking at making changes to," MacAlister said.He acknowledged that the current system did not strike the right balance between safeguarding biological relatives' medical privacy and enabling adopted people to access information relevant to their own health."We do need to change how we keep, retain, and share medical records," he said.Authorities in England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales all make provisions for adoptees to access their medical history, but the way this operates in practice can vary hugely in the different nations.None of the four nations gives patients the legal right to that information.But they advise that when a new clinical record is created for an adopted child, enough information must be kept to support continuity of care.NHS England said depending on the circumstances of an adoption there may be a need to "protect from disclosure any information about a third party". But it added that it is important any new NHS records, if created, contain sufficient information to allow for a continuity of care.For Courtney-Grace, her own diagnosis means her five-month-old daughter will now be closely monitored.Cord blood was collected when Tine was born, and it will be tested for the genetic condition when she is five. If she has inherited it, a plan will be put in place."She has the medical information," Courtney-Grace says. "She can say, 'My mum has this'".A list of organisations in the UK offering support and information with some of the issues in this story is available at BBC Action Line

schema.headline: What happens when you grow up not knowing your family medical history?

title: Palantir AI probe leads to Met Police volunteer chief's dismissal
description: The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to cop
body: The Metropolitan Police has fired the head of its Special Constabulary after Palantir's AI monitoring uncovered that he had used his work phone to copy intimate images of a woman.Special chief officer James Deller, who led the force's volunteer officers, was dismissed following a misconduct hearing on Friday.The Met said investigators used lawful business monitoring and Palantir's Foundry system, which uses artificial intelligence (AI), to find the misconduct by Deller.Cdr Pete Stevens said: "SCO Deller failed to meet that bar. His actions were an abuse of the trust put in him and it is right that he is no longer able to serve in policing."Investigators found that in July and August 2025, Deller used his police-issued phone to take photos of two intimate images that had been sent to his personal phone.The pictures had been sent using WhatsApp's "view once" feature, which makes them disappear after they are opened.He then sent the copied images back to his personal device before deleting them from his work phone.The misconduct was discovered during a week-long operation called Project Galatasaray, which used the AI technology in a bid to identify corruption and professional misconduct within the Met.Deller will be added to the College of Policing's barred list, meaning he will not be able to serve in policing again.Stevens added: "The vast majority of Met officers and staff serve London with dedication and integrity, and they rightly expect robust action against the small minority who abuse their position and undermine public trust."That is particularly true of those who serve in the Special Constabulary. They are volunteers who selflessly give up their time to keep London safe. "They deserve to be led by people who demonstrate the highest standards in all parts of their lives."In April, the Metropolitan Police Federation urged officers to be "extremely cautious" about carrying Met-issued devices while off duty after the force upgraded its Lawful Business Monitoring software.The federation's general secretary, Matt Cane, said staff had not been told the upgrade included the introduction of Palantir's artificial intelligence technology, appearing to mark its first deployment to monitor Met systems.In May, Metropolitan Police Deputy Commissioner Matt Jukes told the London Assembly's Police and Crime Committee that officers were not under any "additional surveillance in the workplace" after the force began using AI in a bid to root out bad behaviour.He said the Met had considered the reputational risks of using the "divisive" technology, but added that it helped identify "unacceptable, dishonest, corrosive behaviours" among officers.The London Mayor's Office for Policing and Crime (Mopac) blocked the Met from signing a two-year contract with Palantir to provide artificial intelligence technology for criminal investigations.Mopac said the force had failed to set out its procurement strategy, describing this as a "clear and serious breach" of procedure.Palantir is now suing Mopac, alleging it unlawfully blocked the deal after taking the company's "values and ethics" into account, which it said was an "irrelevant consideration.Palantir, founded by controversial tech billionaire Peter Thiel, holds contracts with a number of UK public bodies, including the NHS and the Ministry of Defence.Prime Minister Andy Burnham is currently facing growing pressure from Labour MPs and trade unions to end government contracts with Palantir.Former Labour deputy leader Tom Watson, who recently joined the company, warned against "mob rule" in government procurement.Lord Watson told BBC Radio 4's Political Thinking With Nick Robinson: "One of the things I'd say to my former colleagues is, 'Do you want to let the rule of law lead procurement practice, or do you want to let mob rule lead procurement practices?'"Because you get yourself in a lot of trouble if you go down on the latter one."Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

title: We're saving £100 a month for our kids but they won't get it until they're 57
description: Image source, Richard BrainImage caption, Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices nowByElizab
body: Image source, Richard BrainImage caption, Richard Brain says that opening pensions for his young children means a few financial sacrifices nowByElizabeth AndersonBusiness reporterRichard and Caitlin Brain's two children are aged just 20 months and five months respectively, yet mum and dad have already set up pensions for them.The Brains, who live in Swansea, south Wales, are paying £50 a month into each of their kids' accounts. It's money that the children won't be able to access until they are 57, under current UK private pension fund rules., externalSo the eldest will have to wait until 2082, and the youngest until 2083.Despite the wait, Richard, 30, is convinced that he and Caitlin, 28, are doing the right thing."Paying into their pensions means we can play a part in their future far beyond our own years. And the money has decades to grow."'We don't eat out as often as we used to'Richard's financial knowledge is explained by the fact he works for an investment firm. Caitlin is currently on maternity leave from her job working for the local council.He earns less than £90,000 a year, while she currently doesn't have an income as she has not yet returned to work after her statutory maternity pay of £194 a week ended.In addition to their children's pensions, Richard and Caitlin have also set up Junior ISA savings accounts for them, and pay in £60 a month per child - money the kids will be able to access when they turn 18.The couple believe this is the best of both worlds – the ISAs could help their children with university costs, starting a business or a house deposit, while the pensions are intended to provide financial security much later in life.Paying a combined £220 a month into their kids' funds, in addition to £200 into their own private pensions and savings, the couple say they must live more frugally than in the past."We're not on the breadline, but investing this money does mean doing a little less," says Richard. "We don't eat out as often as we used to, which as foodies is a pain."And we don't go as big for one another on birthdays and Christmas so that we can still do it for the kids."'I want to retire earlier so this will help'Pensions for children, also called Junior self-invested personal pensions (SIPPs), were introduced in the UK in 2001. You can pay in a maximum of £2,880 per year, which the government will then top up with £720 tax relief to make a total £3,600.The popularity of Junior SIPPs has grown, industry figures show. One provider, Hargreaves Lansdown, says that in the 12 months to April 2026 it had seen two and a half times as many accounts open, external as in the same period a year earlier. Another, Fidelity, says it has seen the number of accounts more than triple since December 2023.While giving their kids a pensions head start is a powerful incentive for some parents, how do the children themselves feel about not being able to touch the money for potentially 50 years or more?Fifteen-year-old Hugo Thompson from Manchester seems unfazed. His parents, who work in finance, have been paying the maximum amount into his Junior SIPP for the past 10 years."The money invested means perhaps I'll be ahead when I'm older," he says. "So I won't have to put quite so much of my own money in! I want to retire earlier than the state pension age so this will all help."Hugo's mother Annabel, who works in finance, also saves into a Junior ISA for him, but says she still also invests into her own pension and savings. "For me, Junior SIPPs should only be considered once you feel you have enough money of your own," she says.Image source, Hugo ThompsonImage caption, Hugo Thompson is happy to wait until he is at least 57 to access the pension fundFor parents who can afford it, the money can grow substantially before the child can access it, says Jemma Slingo, a pensions specialist at Fidelity."Paying in £50 a month from birth, including tax relief, the family would contribute £10,800 over those 18 years. The pot could grow to around £135,000 by retirement. That's the real power of starting early - relatively modest amounts can have an exceptionally long time to compound."It's not just British parents that are opening long-term investments for their children.In July this year, US President Donald Trump launched a new retirement investment scheme for children called Trump Accounts.Families, friends and employers can contribute up to $5,000 (£3,800) per year per child. The difference with the UK is that the children can access the funds from when they turn 18, although withdrawals are subject to taxes and a possible 10% penalty if made before the age of 59 and a half.Wally Luckeydoo, a personal finance teacher at Smyrna High School in Tennessee, has opened Trump Accounts for his two children, aged four and three.Image source, Wally LuckeydooImage caption, Wally Luckeydoo says he is giving his children a "financial head start""My dad passed away when I was very young, and my mom did everything she could to provide for us, often with just the bare minimum," says Wally."For much of my adult life, I have felt like I was trying to catch up financially, particularly because of significant student loan debt."I don't necessarily think of this as specifically saving for my kids' retirement. I think of it as giving them a head start and helping change the trajectory of our family financially."Get in touchHave you been affected by the issues raised in this story?Get our flagship newsletter with all the headlines you need to start the day. Sign up here.

title: Greek takeaways: What did we learn from England's World Cup play-off win in Crete?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sarina Wiegman has led England to back-to-back European titlesByBBC Sport women’s football news reporter at P
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Sarina Wiegman has led England to back-to-back European titlesByBBC Sport women’s football news reporter at Pankritio StadioEngland came away from Greece with a valuable first-leg lead in their Women's World Cup qualifying play-off - but what did we learn?Sarina Wiegman's side are looking to secure their place in Brazil next year but have to navigate the play-offs after finishing runners-up in their qualification group.The back-to-back European champions won 3-1 in Crete on Friday night and will need to finish the job against Greece on Tuesday in Leicester (19:30 BST).The winner of the tie faces Ukraine or Slovakia in round two to decide who will head  to Brazil.Le Tissier takes her opportunityLucy Bronze withdrew from the squad with a minor injury earlier this week, handing a rare opportunity to Manchester United captain Maya le Tissier.The defender is a key player for her club but struggles to break into the England team with Bronze understandably a tough figure to displace. Wiegman sees Le Tissier as a right-back as opposed to a centre-back - which is her position at United - and that meant she was handed a start against Greece.Making her 15th cap, Le Tissier was a standout performer and was rewarded with her first international goal in the 63rd minute, providing optimism for a future without 34-year-old Bronze."As soon as we were in possession, she was higher on the pitch and she already came close to a couple of moments with crosses," said Wiegman."I'm very happy for her and for the whole team because that was an important goal."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Maya le Tissier scored her first goal for England in the second halfSloppiness creeps in againIt was just England's third win in their past eight competitive away games.A 3-1 victory is a pleasing result, but given the gulf in class, Wiegman admitted frustrations at not keeping a clean sheet.There were familiar lapses in concentration defensively that gave Greece opportunities to pounce. Ioanna Papatheodorou struck the crossbar in the first half, before teeing up Kallisti Brouksair for their goal later on.Those chances came from England errors and the lack of clean sheet means the door remains open for Greece in the second leg."That's up to us. We have to show up on Tuesday, play a good game and then we should be better than Greece," said Wiegman. "Of course we want to take some more distance [in the scoreline], that's absolutely true, but at the same time we won and that's the most important thing. "Sometimes we played really well and sometimes we were a bit sloppy. We were a bit frustrated as we wanted to do that better. "We want to show more than winning, we want to play really well too."A glimpse of the future With victory secure, Wiegman was able to hand a debut to 18-year-old Erica Meg Parkinson, as well as Liverpool captain Grace Fisk.Fisk, 28, had waited more than six years for her debut, having received her first England call-up in 2020 but Parkinson has broken through at pace this season.The teenager was unexpectedly named in Wiegman's squad in March, having only made the jump up to England's Under-23s a few months earlier.She secured a move to the United States this summer, joining North Carolina Courage from Portuguese side Valadares Gaia, and came on in the 85th minute.This week defender Esme Morgan said: "She's a really intelligent player. She has incredibly good movement and timing, picking up pockets for players to find her."She's really comfortable receiving [the ball] in tight spaces, she's strong holding off players, very aggressive in her tackling and wins back a lot of balls. "I've been really impressed with Erica since she came into camp and also from playing against her in the National Women's Soccer League."Who is England's number 10?Image source, Getty ImagesParkinson's debut added to the debate of who Wiegman's preferred number 10 is. She is one of many options available, including Chelsea forward Lauren James, who was given a creative, free role against Greece.James showed flashes of quality and nonchalantly lobbed goalkeeper Fafailia Petaloti from 30 yards in the first half, but her effort was ruled out for offside.Other options include Manchester City's Grace Clinton and Manchester United's Ella Toone, who were both recalled to the squad to cover injuries with Aston Villa's Lucia Kendall among those to drop out.Laura Blindkilde Brown started in that position with James in Crete, while Beth Mead and Jess Park have also played there before.The position was a difficult one for Wiegman to nail down at Euro 2025 and more than a year later, the question of who is England's best number 10 remains."I see there is a lot of competition in that position, where we have a lot of options with different players, who have different qualities," said Wiegman."You can call it a question mark but I call it many options. Today we had two 10s and sometimes three. [James] was one of them."Job done in strange circumstancesLocal media had questioned why the game wasn't being played in Greece's capital city Athens.And there was an eerie atmosphere with fewer than 4,000 fans in the 26,000-capacity stadium in Heraklion, Crete.The Lionesses are also not used to being in play-offs, a route they are having to take after finishing runners-up to world champions Spain in their qualifying group.But Georgia Stanway, this year's top scorer for England, once again turned up when they needed her to and she opened the scoring after a neat, incisive passing move, in a frustrating first half. That was the spark England needed as they lacked ruthlessness and failed to capitalise on their dominance - an aspect of their game that needs improving."I think we made it a bit harder. Greece were well prepared and disciplined. We struggled when they tried to press us," added Wiegman."We could have scored more than the three goals. There are lots of things to take. I have seen some fluid moments but I want more. "The final ball, final cross and the positions can be better. Of course, we are working on that. We have an opportunity to improve that on Tuesday."

schema.headline: Greek takeaways: What did we learn from England's World Cup play-off win in Crete?

title: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
description: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nationImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of thousand
body: 'Everyone hates the police' – what France's school protests reveal about a divided nationImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Hundreds of thousands of students have protested across France since the end of last monthByNick BeakeEurope correspondentAs dustbins burn and students chant "everyone hates the police" in the French city of Lille, one teenager explains why he and his friends have taken to the streets."There aren't even enough chairs. We have to go and find some at the start of every lesson," the 16-year-old, who did not want to give his name, says of his school."We've got 50 minutes to eat at lunchtime but there are 2,000 of us that need to get through the canteen."He is one of hundreds of thousands of students who have protested across France since the end of last month over staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycées, secondary schools attended by 15 to 18-year-olds.Despite the government's apparent attempts to make concessions, the students show no sign of backing down."They have armies, they have the police, they have the powers," says Massicella, 18, as she marches through Lille. "But we have the mass population."The protests, which have turned violent, have become a focal point in France's polarised politics, with all sides accusing the other of escalating tensions. As a presidential election approaches, politicians on both the hard right and hard left have sought to capitalise on the unrest and on what many see as the government's inability to resolve the crisis.Image caption, Massicella, second left, and her friends have been protesting in LilleThe protests - ignited at the Lycée Antoine-de-Saint-Exupéry in the deprived Paris suburb of Créteil - have struck a chord across the country.Videos of rats scuttling through corridors in other lycées soon hit social media, providing striking symbols of the discontent. Other videos on TikTok and Instagram showed broken toilets, holes in walls and mouldy ceilings across the country. Students have complained of unbearable heat in the summer and freezing classrooms in the winter.The anger has also focused on long school hours, chronic staff shortages, overcrowded classes and a deeply unpopular university admissions system.Figure caption, Watch: Marseille school students explain why they're protestingThe problem for the French government - which became clearer as we spoke to dozens of pupils this week - is that even if a tiny minority of schools have a problem with rodents, a very large number of pupils believe their own education is failing them.On Tuesday, the government said 250,000 people marched, most of them young. The trade unions said it was more like half a million.But it is not just students taking to the streets - their teachers are joining them.Secondary school teacher Marine Monins, who joined the demonstrations in Lille, shows us a laminated timetable which she says illustrates the problem.It has become normal for pupils to start at 8am and finish as late as 6pm, but the days are punctuated by hours-long gaps because of bad planning and staff shortages.When lessons do go ahead, the classes are typically packed with 35 pupils (by comparison, the average secondary school class in England has fewer than 23 pupils)."It's now impossible to give every child the attention they deserve," Monins explains.Image caption, Teachers, including Marine Monins and Marjorie Roussel, have joined their students in calling for changeOn Thursday, the French government made its first sign of ceding ground to protesters, with a promise of 3,000 extra supply teachers in the coming days.Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has said by the end of October there will be a plan unveiled to respond to the crisis. Ministers have said they could look again at resources for schools within next year's squeezed budget.But this has been met with a collective shrug at barricaded school gates across the country."It goes beyond having decent toilets in schools," lycée student Alcidor says in Paris, under the statue of Marianne at Place de la République, a place synonymous with protest."It's strong anger from the youth in France that doesn't feel represented, that feels abandoned, that feels unheard and is scared of what's coming in the future."Image source, ReutersImage caption, Police have been accused of heavy-handed tacticsThe unrest has resulted in widespread arrests and injuries.So far, almost 7,000 people have been detained during the disorder with more than 85% being children, according to the interior ministry.More than 700 police officers have been injured in the past three weeks.But rights groups and unions accuse the police of resorting to heavy-handed tactics against minors, including the use of batons, tear gas and non-lethal flash-ball guns. At least 200 pupils have been injured, along with dozens of teachers.A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators in the northern city of Lens.Reports of how the teenager sustained the injury differ. A police union source cited by the AFP news agency said the boy appeared to have picked up a sting-ball grenade fired by riot police, which then exploded in his hand. However, a witness told local media that the teenager did not pick up the grenade.A teacher at the boy's school, Bastien Riez, who is also a union rep, believes that current police tactics could irrevocably damage the relationship with France's youth."For many, this is their first experience of democracy and protest, and they are met with police and a sham of social dialogue and democracy. I fear that many young people will stop believing in this so-called democracy altogether."Police have since been banned from using stun grenades at school protests.Image caption, Kaspar says strangers have been hijacking some protestsBut Parisian pupil Kaspar, 15, speaks of his fear when coming face-to-face with police in full riot gear. He says he and his friends have been protesting peacefully, but strangers were hijacking their protests."These people are coming just to shoot fireworks at police officers and they run. This is not the message we want to send to the world."Police chiefs say violence, directed by agitators who have no link to the schools, is making their job incredibly hard.Michel Chaballier, deputy secretary-general of the National Police Commissioners' Union (SCPN), says he fears the "political climate has been radicalised", and it was more and more difficult to have a calm, constructive public debate ahead of the national vote next spring."Police officers find themselves caught in the middle of this social tension, which is sometimes fuelled by irresponsible politicians," he says. "That's a shame, because I think this country deserves better."Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Marine Le Pen has condemned damage to schoolsThe protests have become another bruising battleground in France's culture wars, with leaders of the hard left and right seeking to capitalise.More than three-quarters of under-30s in France interviewed for an Ipsos survey conducted for Aix-Marseille University this week said they were worried about the state of their country.But many people have a more profound and wider concern about just how dramatically the middle ground in France is eroding, leaving a chasm in the political landscape.The education crisis is symptomatic of this but also threatens to act as an accelerant.Most polling suggests more and more French citizens are looking to political extremes for answers to their problems – whether they are linked to education, the economy, identity or immigration.Marine Le Pen of the hard right National Rally is the frontrunner in the 2027 presidential race.Next, neck and neck, are Édouard Philippe and Jean-Luc Mélenchon.Philippe was a prime minister in President Emmanuel Macron's first term and has since founded a centre-right party called Horizons.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Jean-Luc Mélenchon has been supportive of the demonstrationsJean-Luc Mélenchon, a veteran hard-left politician and founder of France Unbowed (LFI), has been a prominent older face among the students at rallies over the past three weeks.Opponents have accused him of provoking and profiting from the unrest, while he counters that only his party truly represents the French youth.He claims the current movement that has emerged from the schools protest is the most potent since 1968, when huge demonstrations almost brought down the government of President Charles de Gaulle. At its height, 10 million workers were on the streets before fresh elections led to the revolt fizzling out, but not before carving an indelible memory in French social history.Despite being born more than four decades later, an exasperated generation of French teenagers are looking to the past for inspiration."I personally want to reproduce 1968!" Massicella declares in Lille, as she nears the end of the protest march.Le Pen has stayed away from the protests and her most notable interventions have come in condemning the damage to schools, which is said to run into the millions of euros.She has also suggested that parents of children who have committed the vandalism should pay for repairs.The principle of casseur-payeur – those who break have to pay – has been an impassioned topic that has dominated French media this week.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, The 1968 protests have carved an indelible memory in French social historyThe problem for President Macron is that there is no quick fix.This is not a scenario where there is an unpopular piece of legislation that can be withdrawn in a hasty reverse ferret the prime minister is tasked with performing. That was the case with the gilets jaunes – the relentless protest in high vis jackets over a fuel tax rise nearly a decade ago.Wholesale reform of the education system would cost billions – in new classrooms, new facilities, new teachers – and take years to achieve.And changes that may seem more easily done – such as a reduction of the length of the school day – would be hugely problematic to implement logistically.What is more, any proposals which appease the students and end the current protests would have to be agreed at a time when France's finances are in a mess.The cost of servicing the national debt each year has now exceeded the core state education budget. Under the 2027 draft budget, there will be a 1.7% rise in education spending - but this is an under-inflation increase.Le Pen has vowed to cut public spending even further if she enters the Élysée Palace.She is banking that her promises to cut debt, curb migration and restrict certain benefits to French citizens will eclipse any criticism over her position on the protesting pupils.For her, discipline, a traditional curriculum and pride in France's history should be the defining features of every classroom.Image source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Many students have said they will not back down from protestingBut many students are showing little sign of backing down from another French tradition."In France, we have this tradition and history of revolting," says Alcidor in Paris."That's the way we gained our rights and the way we will always gain them. That's our spirit."As the rain came outside the Lycée Voltaire central in Paris this week, the reality of having been up early once again to block the main gate started to kick in and the energy of the crowd dipped.But not for long.A huge cheer erupted as a senior teacher unlocked the hulking front door and poked her head out into the street."The canteen is still open."The hunger for better schools among France's youth and better days for everyone else will not be so easily sated.Additional reporting by Bruno Boelpaep and Manon Prat

schema.headline: France's school protests are about more than broken classrooms
